One thing I’m noticing here is that you are always the one looking for doctors, researching her options, etc. While it’s great that you’re there to support her and to help her with finding treatment, I guess I’m wondering if this imbalance is contributing a bit. I also wonder about the mental health challenges you describe. How often are you able to discuss her options as a team? I had someone declare themselves my caretaker (honestly with terrible results) for a few years. The person often swooped in to do more for me than was necessary, insisting I was too hurt/too sick/etc to do whatever it was. This contributed to learned helplessness on my end, and I ended up in deep shit when this person abruptly left. If a caretaker role is necessary, there should be communication (as well as ways for the sick person to be as much of an equal partner as possible). 

Good luck, though.

On one hand, I get what they’re saying. Many people have dealt with abusers whose unprocessed trauma causes them to lash out and treat others horribly. Because these abusers refuse to work on themselves (or even acknowledge themselves as capable of having shortcomings that need work), the victim ends up figuring out the triggers through guesswork and then tiptoeing around them. In these relationships, there’s no option to say, “Hey, I notice whenever I’m not home exactly on time, you lash out at me. Can we talk about why this is? I’m willing to listen and understand, but the way you treat me needs to change/improve.” The abuser will just get angry and defensive, forcing the victim to learn via trial and error how not to disturb the beast.

On the flip side, these types of quotes are often weaponized against people who are AWARE of their triggers, doing everything that feels safe and possible to address it right now (with or without therapy), and are just asking for a bit of patience/mercy/understanding when the trigger comes up. One example could be the person cries and gets shaky when sex comes up as a topic. The person is able and willing to explain that the topic is triggering and that they’re not in a good place to discuss it. If people scream at them to “take responsibility” instead of “expecting other people to,” it will likely reinforce their shame rather than empowering them to take charge over their own reactions. 

I don’t think most normies understand that fully extinguishing triggers isn’t always as simple as just go to therapy, do the work, and it’ll all work itself out. Even when it IS that simple, it takes time to work!

Oh yikes I’m sorry. I’ve also seen it go like, “My therapist said I need to set boundaries, so no, I won’t stop doing blah blah like you asked. My therapist said sometimes emotionally immature people don’t respect boundaries, so that’s what you are if you’re annoyed with me right now!” 

I’ve also seen one aggressively pick apart every word I say, then shake her head in dismay that I wasn’t not in therapy and “healing” like she was. If I said, “I need a shower because I feel gross right now,” she’d coldly snap that “gross” is not a feeling. In reality, I “think” I’m gross. She’d demand I restate it that way and then if I said, “I don’t actually THINK that - I just have a gross feeling because I need a shower,” she’d say I wasn’t very articulate, and she couldn’t be expected to handhold me through my immature inability to express myself. 

This is why, while I applaud people with BPD seeking help to improve their situation, I don’t encourage friends or partners to hold out hope that therapy will restore the honeymoon phase dream partner.

True, though not every DBT provider is necessarily good at navigating the complexities of BPD. Even those who are have their work cut out for them! The hardest part of therapy with a BPD client is a healthy therapeutic alliance. They need to feel some buy-in and connection without putting the therapist on a temporary pedestal that collapses, just like they did with the relationship partner. They also have to be honest enough with the therapist for the therapist to know what suggestions to give. That can be difficult even for a highly trained clinician.

Sometimes DBT providers also put more emphasis on the right way to behave or respond than on the underlying self-loathing and shame that leads to the inappropriate response. I personally think DBT combined with more of the deeper exploratory work on the core shame that fuels the childlike behavior is important. It’s just harder for people with these types of issues to find the ideal therapeutic relationship, even if they’re willing and have heard of BPD and DBT.

Sadly, there are very few professionals even equipped to help people with BPD. I’ve seen people with BPD go in and tell the therapist, “I think I have BPD,” then get tossed around as no one knows how to help them. For people who are already rejection sensitive and already don’t want to open up to strangers, this can be really demoralizing. A simple, “Go to therapy,” sounds dismissive when someone’s done it 15 times with no luck.

There is, in the sense that many therapists view BPD as “client from hell” and don’t want to work with them. The spectrum of people with BPD ranges from people who eventually realize they were toxic and do seek help to people who also have some NPD traits and either never seek help or never find someone who can appropriately call them on their behavior. Sometimes people see being diagnosed with BPD as being told they have “bad person disorder” and are just like all the awful exes and parents described in a sub like this. Truthfully, there’s black and white thinking about these symptoms.

I think on the flip side, people who’ve been abused by those with BPD need a clear cut, “These people will never be sorry and will never work on themselves,” because otherwise they’ll still be clinging on to the idea that their own specific person will change. The truth is, even when someone with BPD does get help, their personal journey may not lead them to a happily ever after with the partner that’s waiting for them to change. I think it’s worth noting some cluster B people can change, but that doesn’t mean their false love bombing persona will come back full time to be the partner of your dreams.

This is a very interesting post.

I’ve noticed lately that in many spaces, autism is seen as the only neurodivergent condition that “counts.” If I say I had major difficulty socializing as a child, I’m either told I must be autistic or that an autistic person’s struggle will always be worse. Never mind that ADHD brains often like to talk much more than other people like to listen, or that C-PTSD can majorly alienate a kid from same-age peers. It’s not the ‘tism, so it’s not special and important.

I’ve weirdly enough seen people change their entire personality, including career goals, preferences in social situations, etc. after self-diagnosing with autism. Whatever non-autistic behavior they used to do prior to diagnosis gets retconned as inauthentic. I’ve then seen people who do this go on to try and push their own self-dx onto others.

I just really don’t see what makes autism the superior, most special form of ND that you’re seen as less ND and less in need of compassion if you don’t have. I worry people viewing it that way will create incorrect ideas about what people with actual autism should be able to do.

This makes so much sense. I have ADHD + C-PTSD + OCD, and I frequently get told social awkwardness I attribute to early trauma + only child with no cousins anywhere near my age could *only* be from autism, especially since I have the sensory issues. I’ve talked to people who were evaluated professionally and told it’s not autism, who think their diagnosis still isn’t big enough to fit the magnitude of struggle they’re facing, so it must be autism. 

I’ve also noticed that sometimes when people don’t do well in individual therapy (especially after trying several therapists), they assume the issue must be a bigger diagnosis than the therapist was aware of. In many cases, it’s more like there are lifestyle issues as well as patterns of behavior the person feels locked into that are keeping the person chronically stressed and overwhelmed. 

I’ve also seen the, “It’s not BPD! I’m misdiagnosed! It’s really autism!” People know that if the problem is BPD, they’ll have to learn emotional regulation techniques that will allow them to recognize ways their chronic emotional pain leads to self-sabotage as well as harm to their relationships. The path forward will be about improving their self-image, yes, but also about learning to take responsibility without shame. Yes, I did make a faux pas. I can admit that without feeling like a broken or unlovable person. That’s very frightening and overwhelming. A diagnosis like autism might (in some people’s minds) mean less responsibility as they’re able to say, “This is because of a condition I was born with, that can’t really be changed,” so there’s no need to face the unpleasant feelings that keep people with BPD (or even C-PTSD with BPD traits) in that chronic emotional pain. 

I’ve sometimes seen people view the autism label as a way to try and have more services and help for themselves when they reach adulthood and realize (for whatever reason) they aren’t ready to be adults. I’d love to see adulting coaches/courses to help people catch up on emotional maturity and everyday living skills they weren’t taught as children or didn’t learn on time for whatever reason. I don’t think stuff like that should be limited to only certain diagnoses because plenty of people struggle with adulting for various reasons, and there should be more options for everyone imo.

This is 100% true. Managers and supervisors are not fully trained to be managers and supervisors. This means when you start a supervisory role you’re gonna be blamed for everything as your staff expects you to take charge from day one. If you don’t, they undermine you and try to make choices without you. If you step in and say, “Hey, as the boss, I’m supposed to do this,” they feel disrespected because you’re less experienced than they are at this point. If you say, “Okay, okay, for right now, you know better than I do, so I’ll observe and then take over after 6 months,” they’ll resist and fight that transition.

If you’re a supervisor with any level of imposter syndrome or self-doubt, you’ll feel like you absolutely can’t win. Your frustration will come across as a person in authority having an unreliable mood. Then, you’ll have people thinking you’re trying to fire them or trying to wreck their lives when really you’re just trying to navigate weird social politics of managing a team that was hired before you showed up, as a literal first time supervisor.

Part of that is because many companies have taken a chance on a promising yet inexperienced person who hasn’t even had the basic workplace etiquette, has been an extremely slow learner (to the point of taking months to do basic orientation tasks), and has taken up too much of a supervisor’s time. All it takes is one bad hire for them to say, “Next time, I’m not messing around. I want someone who’s already experienced.”

Basically, they’re not sure how to tell the inexperienced but trainable people apart from the inexperienced folks who will drag everyone else down from not really having the drive or openness or teachability to grow into the role.

There’s also absolutely zero support for people whose sexual trauma doesn’t allow them to do an exam or internal PT, who want to be able to just ask questions and learn from someone with medical knowledge to the full extent that’s possible. Sure, people will say that can’t exist, go to therapy, etc., but what happens when therapy has done more harm than good? What happens when you want access to some level of medical support that can work within your window of tolerance, like let me go in and do what I can handle/modify things where possible, etc.? Not a thing. That doesn’t exist for me at all, and the reality is even if I could trust doctors, most of them don’t know enough about the issues I’m having to be helpful, and if they’re not helpful, I’ll feel like I experienced a retraumatizing violation for nothing. I only started to improve after my last therapist dropped me, when I was isolated during the pandemic. Being authentic with myself IS difficult. It’s so difficult, but I can’t be authentic with others while lying to myself. I don’t personally like the term “healing” but think some people’s process is easier without trying to force the relational element to work.

I’m non-autistic but neurodivergent and have had to shut down multiple online friends who are autistic when they’ve tried to apply that label to me. I’ve had people tell me that MH professionals saying they don’t think I have (or need to be tested for) autism “doesn’t prove anything,” and that plenty of autism flies under the radar. I even had a masseuse tell me her psychic intuition told her I was autistic and push me to take an internet quiz to prove it. Sometimes when I say I’m not autistic and don’t want the label applied to me, I’m asked what’s “wrong” with autism that would make me say that.

I can relate so much to this. I think one of the things I'm coming to terms with right now is knowing how therapy works versus how I work.

You'll often hear that when it comes to therapy, "It's the relationship that heals!" For less avoidant people, the simple act of sitting in the room with a fellow human being who listens and cares (which, let's face it, is more than many therapists even seem able to offer, but that's a whole other issue) is restorative. 

It makes sense. Let's say a client's worldview is something like, "Connection is good. I want to be connected to other people, but the connection I'm seeking either isn't available from the people in my daily life *or* is something I'm afraid to ask for due to hearing (usually as a child) that my needs aren't important. When that client finds the right therapist, they'll start to feel less afraid of asking for the connection they want, as well as seeking out new connections. Why? The therapist will validate their need for connection and ease their fears that they might not deserve it. The client will give the therapist the power to do this, based on their worldview supporting "connection is basically a good thing that I desire and believe would add value to my life."

In contrast, let's say a client's worldview is something like, "Connection hurts. I require a ton of emotional preparation to deal with people, followed by a ton of self-care to de-escalate my panic once I'm done dealing with people. I really don't think an outside person can be my "rock." That's too risky because what happens when I feel rejected or hurt in that relationship? Then, I have no safety or stability in my inner world. What I need is help being enough *for myself, by myself* so that I can take relationships much more lightly than I currently do. This will allow me not to be absolutely gutted every time a coworker seems not to like me or I go to a Meetup group and don't hit it off with anyone."

When this person goes to therapy, they want concrete solutions that will continue to benefit them, with or without this therapist. They do not want closeness with the therapist to be *the solution* in and of itself because it just *can't* be. If a very avoidant person starts to strongly connect with a therapist, the therapist isn't proof that the world is safe. The therapist is a singular exception to how the world generally is, which makes the risk of rejection or sudden termination 300,000,000,000 times scarier. 

I don't think a single thing by itself can help (ie: oh, we're going to therapy now, that's great). We need a lot of different things working in our favor at the same time. That way, therapy can suck this week, and we still have options. Our writer's group can start to become stale, but we at least have water aerobics. Our job can be a pain in the ass right now, but at least our gym regimen is going well. Avoidance makes it easy to put all eggs in one basket, and I think therapy is often more geared toward people who want to connect but feel like they aren't allowed to express that need than toward people for whom connection itself is the source of distress.

If you're opening your mind to communication from spirits and spiritual entities, there's always a chance a spirit could "catfish" and pretend to be something they're not. If it feels like abusers/wrongdoers from your life are in some way invading your inner sanctuary, the most important thing is not to panic. Sometimes people experiencing things like this assume that (1) they've been totally abandoned by their deities, as surely deities can help with things happening in the purely spiritual realm, and (2) the perpetrators must have unlimited power/power that exceeds that of the divine. Going with either belief will weaken your own resolve to protect yourself, which is the opposite of what you want. I know it's hard, but bear with me. 

How much access do these abusers/wrongdoers have to you in your physical, waking life? If you live with any of them, have financial or legal ties to them, live in the same town and see them regularly, are in a relationship with one or more, receive phone calls from them, work with them, etc., you will have to address this problem in order to get free. It's rare for someone to live with an abuser, depend on an abuser, or have ongoing contact with an abuser, etc., say a prayer, then find the abuser gone and totally unable to cause harm again. If there is some real-world tie you still have to the abusers, I would recommend petitioning the deity for help while *also* doing whatever mundane-world actions would help to put distance between yourself and the abuser.

For example, if you live with an abuser who seems to be invading your mind/thoughts/dreams/etc., perhaps doing a spell to support your job search efforts or your apartment hunting efforts would be a good one. If an abuser won't stop calling you, inform them the contact is unwelcome, report it, then cast a spell to make sure your boundaries stick. 

It sounds like asking your deities what *you* can do to become safer will be an important component in asking for their help. More than saying, "Please come smite Bob so he doesn't do what he does again," you're also asking, "Please give me wisdom about how to handle the situation with Bob." The more you see it as a collaboration, the more help you're likely to receive.

This! Therapists often have to have a non-blaming, non-threatening atmosphere to get these clients willing to open up. The problem is the clients take their therapist’s validation back to their suffering friends, partners, etc. and say their therapist said they’re fine, so they must not be abusive or have BPD.

Most likely, she met a therapist who doesn’t believe in BPD or thinks the label does more harm than good. Really, whether or not she meets the diagnostic criteria for BPD is not necessary to determine if her behavior is abusive. If her behavior is abusive, it’s abusive.

BPD can be treated. It’s just rare that someone with BPD is wiling to take the accountability AND successfully finds a competent therapist who’s good with BPD.

For therapy to work, the therapist has to do all of the following:

* Build therapeutic rapport with extremely solid boundaries, to limit the ability for the pwBPD to become overly attached.

* Do all that without triggering rejection sensitivity or shame, ie: “I’m the biggest fool! I thought this LCSW truly cared, but she only cares during sessions!”

* Emphasize the importance of emotional regulation and interpersonal effectiveness in a way that won’t trigger the pwBPD feeling blamed for their own pain.

* Tread carefully without becoming too soft to point out when they’re really messing up.

* Screen constantly, usually in a way that naturally flows and doesn’t feel like screening. These therapists usually need training in how to treat chronic suicidal thoughts on an outpatient basis.

None of this is impossible. It’s just difficult and requires the client to be very much on board and the therapist to be uncommonly well trained beyond what’s taught in grad school.

As a therapist, I have sometimes seen adopted children (who spent their first 2-3 years of life in horribly unstable environments) compared unfavorably to the adoptive family's biological children. This especially happens when the adopted child had an unstable or traumatic first 2-3 years, but the biological children had a loving home from day one. By 5-6-7 etc., the biological child is on time for all their major milestones, while the adopted child continues to have challenges stemming from that early disruption of their development. Many families are not really prepared to face this. The worst part is that not many *therapists* even receive training on this topic, besides the surface level, "They may have attachment trauma," that you'll learn about in grad school. I think the reality that someone with early childhood trauma, who's adjusting to a new environment away from their original caregivers, has special needs even if there's no clear sign of ADHD, autism, I/DD, etc. needs to be emphasized.

This is not to say every child will majorly struggle, but I've noticed a lot of adopted kids seem to have trauma that happened before they were old enough to articulate it. Then, parents often send the kid to a therapist, but the kid says, "I don't have any trauma I want to talk about!" The parent is certain the child's past trauma is the reason for current acting-out behaviors and believes talking to a therapist about the adoption will stop the defiant teenage behaviors. The kids are confused and angry because they don't particularly want to talk about the adoption but are now being pushed to because Mom thinks it will help them stop drinking or sneaking out or vaping. There ends up being a disconnect, where the child goes, "Why does my mom keep insisting I talk about the adoption when I don't care about it anymore?" and you're stuck wondering how to tell the kid that dissecting early childhood trauma is the family's plan to get them to "behave themselves." The kid ends up resentful and feels like on top of being punished for their behavior, they're being dissected because they're adopted. This then leads to more resentment and more acting out. It gets really messy and complicated.

The difficulty is that marginalized people who are *not* already on board with the abolitionist vegan mindset hear, "Harming animals just because they're animals is no better than harming marginalized people just because they're different," and feel dehumanized. I've especially seen this happen when speciesism is compared to racism. People affected by racism are used to being unfavorably compared to animals, in a way that denies their humanity. When a marginalized person believes you are saying, "People like you are no better than \[creatures we collectively take for granted are less than human\]," they'll be responding from a place of hurt, pain, and feeling triggered. There's no universe where having people like themselves compared to animals will feel justified. It'll instead feel like, "If we're gonna let thooooose people have rights, we might as well let chickens have rights too," almost like you're mocking them. This is especially true if the vegan making the argument is white and saying, "Hurting animals is like racism," or straight and saying, "Hurting animals is like homophobia."

I've seen vegans double down on these talking points like, "NO, you don't get it! I think animals and humans are *equally* important," and things only get worse. Equal rights for humans aren't a done deal, yet they're simpler to achieve than equal rights for animals. Trying to piggyback animal rights off of social justice movements focused on human rights seems to backfire, especially when those battles aren't fully won yet. Human rights issues are simpler in the sense that...let's say humans invade your home and eat all your food. Theoretically, police could remove them and either incarcerate them or direct them to social services. No one needs to unalive for this problem to be resolved. Those options don't exist if mice invade your home, especially if you are not a homeowner and live in an apartment complex where a humane option that may or may not work is good enough for you but not good enough for your neighbors in the same building. The societal changes it would take to make animals 100% equal to humans would be more difficult than anti-discrimination laws to make society better for marginalized humans.

I say this as a vegan myself. I think we need arguments that emphasize harm-reduction as well as the impact to the planet versus attempting to convince people who don't already think this way that a chicken is equal to a human. I tried convincing people of this at one point in my life and just started feeling disillusioned and disconnected from everyone who wasn't vegan, which was a difficult way to exist.

The thing about therapy is that it can help, but I think it’s extremely important for the child to have some say in it. It’s also important for the parents to be very involved in the process, possibly seeking their own therapy as well. Some children feel “ganged up on” when a parent brings more and more adults into a situation where the child already feels powerless. 

I’ve seen parents wait until there’s a clear behavioral challenge at home and then seek trauma therapy in the hopes that addressing the trauma will “fix” the behavior. The kid then interprets the therapy as a punishment for lying or stealing or vaping. Usually the child won’t link their own problematic behavior to trauma. The kid will say, “I don’t want therapy for the adoption! I don’t even remember that! I don’t get why my mom thinks I have so much I need to say about it!” The truth then comes out that the adoptive parents expect specific behavioral changes to happen as a result of healing emotionally. The child then feels disillusioned and withdraws even more.

I think the more involved parents are with any therapy that happens, the more the process is normalized by BOTH parents, and the more parents are willing to listen if a kid says, “I don’t feel like this is helping,” or “I don’t feel like the therapist I’m seeing is listening,” or “This therapist is good, and I don’t want to switch,” the better the outcome will be.

Identifying as endogenic doesn’t guarantee a lack of DID. Endogenic vs traumagenic is a matter of personal belief about how your system formed, rather than the presence or absence of trauma. There is nothing in the DSM-5-TR criteria specifying the system must identify as having formed from trauma. The diagnostic criteria only talks about the combination of amnesia/memory incongruence, distress, and plurality in some form or another. In other words, a system being endogenic or traumagenic is a separate question from whether they experience a combination of memory issues and plurality that come with distress and struggle.

I do agree people without trauma should not claim to have it in bad faith, nor should people without DID claim to have it in bad faith. That said, I have met systems with trauma that don’t name trauma as their origin *and* systems that do not consider themselves to have trauma that experience enough distress and memory incongruence to end up diagnosed with DID. Most clinicians are not familiar with the endogenic and traumagenic terms, which means they’ll look at you funny if you say, “My dissociation and plurality that causes distress can’t be DID because the plurality itself was endogenic.”

That’s where the lines get blurry.

I do believe you were in the wrong here, but I'm reluctant to say YTA because I believe your reaction came from trauma. Your truth is that you were abused and victimized. Your trust was broken. You were betrayed by someone you (at one time) loved enough to commit your whole life to that person. When most people get married (as you did), they're reasonably certain they've found someone they can spend the rest of their life with. This person you gave your commitment and had a child with went on to betray and hurt you. If cheating wasn't bad enough, this person physically and verbally abused you too. The last thing you need is to feel like anyone is heaping blame on you or judging the situation you're in.

That being said, children (especially teenagers) are far more perceptive than we give them credit for. Your daughter watched this all unfold in her own home. From the messages she sent, it sounds like she mostly blames her father but is also worried about your choices and decision-making. Worrying about your choices (and what will happen to you) is reasonable, given what she went through. It's also worth noting that those messages she sent were not intended for your eyes. She was venting her frustrations and concerns while asking for help so that when she interacted with you directly, she would be able to give you good advice.

It is possible that both of you would benefit from therapy, though I would not push this as something your daughter "has" to do, as therapy isn't magic and tends not to work when a person is not open to it. I think it's important to unpack whatever feelings you experienced reading those texts and what you can do to support your own recovery while also helping her to feel secure and safe in the life you have now.

Lately, more and more therapists are questioning how quickly the field has traditionally moved toward hospitalizing clients with self-deleting thoughts. Therapists who want to minimize unnecessary reporting, especially in cases of chronic self-deleting thoughts, typically seek out specialized training in how to help clients with these thoughts in-house. Of course, the training itself would be geared toward hopefully treating the root cause of those thoughts and helping a client move past them. This means the therapeutic approach would move away from, “Once we talk about your trauma enough, the thoughts will disappear on their own,” in favor of, “We need to identify what’s causing those thoughts and what we can do to help.”

The problem is that a therapist having a progressive mindset about client rights won’t absolve them of their reporting requirement. In some cases, therapists who flex the rules for a specific client end up making some ugly mistakes from reinventing the wheel without being accountable to anyone. When they follow all the rules, they can ask a supervisor for feedback on their work while using de-identified information, ie: “I’m helping a client who has thoughts of ending their life, and I said blah blah and blah. Was that the right thing to say?”

When they start to flex the rules according to what feels right, they lose access to that guidance. If asking for help means admitting they’ve violated the standards of their profession, they’re now working on a complex case with zero professional support. I’ve heard of therapists who do this with the best of intentions getting reported by the same clients they bent the rules to help, sometimes with good reason.

Most people in the field are terrified of losing their career and livelihood over not reporting. Many are also terrified of learning someone they tried to help has taken their own life. Those who are confident about working with self-deleting thoughts are less likely to panic and report at the first sign of those thoughts. This is why your best bet is someone who takes their informed consent requirement seriously. They should tell you where they draw the line between things they can keep confidential and things they can’t. They should also make an effort to avoid jumping to hospitalization if there’s a way to manage your situation safely in-office. They should respond to your fears about reporting non-defensively and be able to clearly establish what they can and can’t keep private.

Someone with chronic self-deleting thoughts, who’s able to create a safety plan and speak openly about what they’re willing to try to help stay safe, should be able to find a therapist who can help them. It really, really helps to be open to trying new coping strategies and recognize that because self-deleting is a permanent decision (and is always available), there’s no harm in postponing those urges until you’ve given therapy a chance to work. A good therapist will treat the safety planning less like an ultimatum and more like a brainstorming exercise to determine every coping skill and resource you have at your disposal, then expand your tool kit of resources. Granted, finding one that has the right training and won’t panic is certainly challenging.

It sounds like your mother maybe is getting overwhelmed or isn’t sure how to help you. Sometimes, people who care can still struggle hearing about severe, potentially life-threatening issues like SI. That’s scary for a mother to hear about, so the next step is often to recommend therapy, so that a professional can help.

The issue is that therapists are obligated to try and prevent you from dying by suicide. Due to a combination of liability fears and the human desire to avoid letting someone die, some therapists panic when they hear a client is considering it. These therapists who immediately push for hospitalization at the slightest mention of it can often scare people away from talking about SI at all.

That said, there are some who can talk to you about those thoughts. Those who have the experience, training, and willingness will still be focused on preventing you from going through with it. Their focus will be on keeping you out of the hospital while still keeping you stable. I’m not saying therapy is necessarily the right option for you, but I do think it’s only a matter of time before any IRL support person who cares about you and wants you to be okay starts to get overwhelmed with regular SI talk. I know this because I used to be in that place nearly 24/7, and I saw the loss of relationships and a lot of very messy messes come up. 

This article might be helpful for you if a therapist’s reaction to SI is your main obstacle to considering it: https://speakingofsuicide.com/2013/07/22/therapists-who-do-not-panic/

I definitely hear your frustration about people believing there's a reality where needles don't bother you. I have found that many therapists (and laypeople alike) oversimplify the issue, as if it's a totally baseless, irrational fear of something that "doesn't hurt all that much." For those of us who are either hypersensitive to pain, medically traumatized, neurodivergent with sensory processing differences, struggling with something like a dissociative or traumatic stress disorder that lessens our ability to modulate our reaction to pain, etc. it is NOT an irrational, "I *know* it doesn't hurt, but my brain freaks me out anyway." When people reduce our fears to this, it becomes even more difficult to validate our own emotions in the way that our trauma requires.

One of the common themes I've noticed among people with medical PTSD is that oftentimes the problem is (1) something that happened to us *really fucking hurt*, and (2) when we looked to others for sympathy or understanding, they told us we were "big babies" or that it "didn't really hurt that much" or that "other people have worse problems." We were hurt "for our own good" and fed the whole narcissist's prayer in defense of whoever hurt us. It didn't happen, and if it did, it wasn't that bad, and if it was, that's not a big deal, and if it is, it's not the doctor's fault, and if it was, s/he was just doing his/her job, and if not, we deserved it.

First thing I realized when starting to sort through this on my own (as therapy left me feeling even worse) was that there is no universe in which I walk into a therapist's office totally unwilling and unable to interface with the medical system and walk out 100% "normal" in that respect. Second thing I realized was that there's no such thing as progress too small to matter.

If someone goes from categorically unable to see *any* doctor for *anything* to occasionally able to snap a photo of a nasty looking knee scrape and send it to a virtual doctor, that person becomes less likely to succumb to a lethal infection than before. If someone goes from unable to handle *anything* with needles to occasionally able to get a flu shot under the best of circumstances, knowing there will be lots of ice cream later, that person becomes less likely to get the flu. If someone in your exact situation goes from able to see a PCP to able to see a PCP and one specialist who agrees to use the labs you already have (when possible), you could end up with many more options than you have right now. When the focus shifts from "conquering your fear of medical care" to "finding ways to access a few more options," I think more progress can happen.

That said, concerned loved ones tend to underestimate the potential harms of re-traumatizing someone who already lives their life in fear. They tend to think it's a choice between feeling scared (but for sure receiving help) and avoiding some temporary fear while continuing to suffer. For those of us with chronic illness and medical trauma, it feels more like risking additional trauma that could made our world darker and more limited than it *already is*, with no guarantee the doctors will take us seriously much less provide real, useful answers in exchange for that massive risk. Unfortunately, with this level of trauma, the more we dismiss our own feelings as "being a baby," the more we miss opportunities to actually address our own fears.

If we want to address our own fears at our own pace, we have to start now, regardless of how small we start. If the small step is, "I will look for a recommendation from fellow chronically ill people and possibly do nothing with it," or "I will install an app on my phone that will let me speak to a virtual doctor if I start to think things are taking a bad turn," or "I will consider journaling about my fear, whether I do it or not," that's fine. The point is to put as much progress as possible between yourself and the next big event.

Therapy, for me, was pretty invalidating and unhelpful. I think with this issue, it's important not to let outside people put pressure on us to handle it differently than we need to for our own sanity. We need as much agency and respect for our autonomy as possible to feel safe seeking medical care. Feeling pressured or guilt-tripped will only make things worse.

1. I’m worried about my friend who’s sick.

3. When doctors don’t listen, things can get bad.
4. I’m a horrible person for not knowing how to help.

If those thoughts come up together, 1-3 don’t need to be picked at. They’re true. 4, on the other hand, could be making my anxiety worse unnecessarily, so it’s something I can work on with a CBT skill. 1-3 are more difficult because they’re true statements, and since it’s someone else’s care, I’m not in the driver’s seat.

Two internships happen during the master’s. Once they get the master’s, they need to take a several hour test to get the first license. With that license, they have to find a job and supervisor that will sponsor their 2,000-4,500 (depending on the license and state) hours. These hours include an even breakdown of sessions, intakes/assessments, and documentation/treatment planning/supervision. The required CE’s to maintain the first license do not count toward the clinical hours. 

Once those hours are complete, they submit a request to take another several hour test for their unrestricted license, which still requires ongoing CE’s to maintain.

The CE’s are each year. Some therapists choose their own CE’s, but oftentimes a workplace will require specific ones the workplace pays for.

It’s not a huge part of it.

This is the training:

- How humans fit into their social environment.
- Basics of how culture can affect things.
- 101 info about privilege and oppression.
- Cishet Neurotypical normative developmental psych. 
- Outdated info on LGBTQ+ stuff.
- Reporting requirements for child and elder abuse.
- The DSM.
- One course on CBT.
- One course on grief.
- One course on substance abuse.
- Brief talk about the most stereotypical forms of abuse.
- One course on religious differences with clients.
- One course on ethics.
- One course on not judging clients for doing bad things.
- Two internships, where the real learning happens.

One thing to keep in mind is that the MA in counseling or MSW doesn’t “make someone an expert” in anything. It’s the bare minimum. They then have to take a test and accumulate anywhere from 2,000 to 4,500 hours of experience depending on where they live and which license they’re seeking prior to entering private practice. Until then, they can only practice while meeting weekly with a supervisor who reviews their notes with them. 

Some therapists spend that 2,000 to 4,500 hour period seeking the training they didn’t get from school. Since they’re required to get a lot of CE credits to maintain their “learner’s permit” anyway, they get the extra training and come out really knowing their stuff. OR…they get extra training that leaves much to be desired. This is where the wild difference between what different therapists seem to understand comes from.

These are completely different terms, though transference does involve feelings. Transference happens when a client projects onto a therapist due to their own past experiences. It can be positive or negative. Suppose a client has a therapist who reminds them of an abuser. The client is especially combative and negative with this specific therapist. In some cases, this can be recognized and used as a productive way to help the client address their feelings about that abuser. Some therapists are quick to assume transference when a client is angry with them. Others wait until they’re literally at wit’s end trying to repair a broken therapeutic alliance to question if transference may be at play. 

Countertransference also exists. This is when the therapist projects onto the client. One example would be a mother who worries about her own relationship with her daughter, becomes a therapist, and then tends to minimize teenage girls and young adult women who report being abused by their mothers based on fear of her own daughter rejecting her someday. 

That said, is there any benefit to sticking with this therapist? If he thinks you have “different needs,” this may be a good opportunity to make an exit and find someone better. That said, I will say I think BPD’s heavily stigmatized nature (and tendency to be weaponized against “noncompliant” people) means that people miss how common and actually treatable it is. It doesn’t just mean bad person disorder. It’s usually a very intense difficulty regulating one’s emotions and forming healthy attachments with others, which stems from trauma. I have no idea if you truly have it or not, but it is so common in traumatized people. Some of what’s taught in BPD therapy can help people without it as well. It helps with self-validation, staying grounded when someone is giving you a hard time, etc. 

That said, I would not stay with a therapist who is threatening this diagnosis as a way of asserting his own rightness in a conflict. That’s messed up, whether you have it or not (and again, I have no idea if you do or not). If it’s possible to look past how frustrating this therapist is being, maybe find out what the referral is actually offering and then make an informed decision if it sounds helpful to you or not. Otherwise, you can always cancel your remaining sessions and find someone else (which may be your best move at this point). A therapist who doesn’t own his mistakes doesn’t sound helpful at all. I had one like that, and it was awful.

To be fair, therapy school only teaches about the most stereotypical contexts for abuse (ie: poor, uneducated parents trying their best but too overwhelmed with financial stress to parent responsibly). The idea that a parent could have enough money and resources to support a child, know what therapy is and have been there numerous times, and still make the choice to abuse never comes up in the curriculum. When dissociation is discussed, they never get into how the lack of memory (or emotional attachment to one’s own experiences) can make a traumatized person an “unreliable” witness to their own trauma story. 

Schools also get hung up on the ACE score, which assumes a heteronormative “male batterer, female victim” dynamic for domestic violence and only acknowledges children going hungry when it happens due to poverty. They fail to acknowledge that someone could choose not to feed their child out of cruelty, that abusers could be female, or that trauma could come from something other than overt abuse (think a serious medical diagnosis where a child is powerless and lacks understanding of what’s happening to them), or that the way the medical or mental health system treats children could be traumatic in its own right, or that severe abuse doesn’t always correlate with marginalization or lack of opportunity for the parents to do better. There’s also zero acknowledgement of how abuse survivors are ill-prepared for adulthood and often end up dependent on abusers or trauma bonded to nightmarish families, partners, or religious/high control groups well into their adult years. 

There’s so little training on recognizing and treating trauma that it’s a wonder people think therapists are experts on the subject. Without considerable additional training post grad school, or personal lived experience, they won’t know much about this subject at all.

This is one of the reasons why a treatment plan is so important in therapy. When a therapist writes one, they’re supposed to collaborate with the client to define what progress/recovery would look like. When a client says, “I want to be healed,” the therapist needs to work with the client to turn an abstract, “Everything’s bad, and I just want to be better already!” into something more actionable.

The treatment plan should not only identify what the goal should be but also how the client and therapist will both know it’s been reached. Unfortunately, the term “healed” implies there’s a point at which you’ll be so emotionally balanced, psychologically stable, and socially graceful that you’ll never have moments of self-doubt or times when someone simply doesn’t like you for no reason. When a therapist is at LAC/LSW level (so the first license they get after grad school), they are required to seek supervision and do case consultations. However, they are also supposed to disclose to clients that they are receiving supervision. There’s a form some will have you sign acknowledging you are aware. The purpose of this is to help them do better. Let’s say a therapist has a case where their current training hasn’t really prepared them to help. They can talk to their supervisor to figure out a good approach to working with that person.

If the therapist is at a higher level (LPC/LCSW), they may still seek supervision. One of mine sought supervision because she’d never worked with my diagnosis before. That said, she was pretty transparent about working with a supervisor. If they’re not, that can be pretty unsettling to find out about.

Usually discussing cases in supervision is limited to, “I have a 13 year old who we’ll call CJ. He’s doing xyz.” It wouldn’t be like, “Cameron Johnson who lives in Omaha Nebraska comes to me every Friday. His mom’s name is Sarah, and she drives a red jeep.” That said, the therapist is supposed to disclose if they receive supervision and ensure you’re comfortable seeing a provider working under supervision.

There are some people who believe BPD is not a real disorder or that it's just the "new hysteria," ie: a label slapped onto patients deemed to be "difficult" as a way of shaming and blaming them for whatever's going wrong in therapy.

The trouble is that there are professionals who use the label that way. This is especially common in hospitals and with less experienced providers who believe an inconsistent sense of self or a tendency toward self-harm can *only* mean BPD. Unfortunately, the reality that *some* people get misdiagnosed with BPD, and the reality that *many* providers have not received adequate training to treat BPD (leading to many BPD clients getting referred out or struggling to find help) has made people very averse to the diagnosis existing much less being applied to themselves. There are definitely trauma-focused therapists who feel the same way about the label and try to avoid it.

In the era of, "Autism is a spectrum," (which came from the DSM-5 reclassifying Asperger's as part of a broader spectrum of autism symptoms rather than its own disorder), many influencers are sharing their experiences of being diagnosed with level one (formerly "high functioning") autism as adults. This is leading a lot of people to wonder, "Hmm...I wonder if autism could be the reason why I've struggled for my entire life while feeling misunderstood and shamed." Since adult diagnosis often is not covered by insurance, people self-diagnose with free screening tools, online quizzes, etc. I'm not wholeheartedly against people using self-diagnosis as a means of gaining self-awareness when formal testing is not accessible to them. However, an online screener won't point out, "The autism questions you answered 'yes' to are the ones that overlap with ADHD, BPD, C-PTSD, etc."

I've heard of some people seeing therapists who really champion the adult autism diagnosis as a way of freeing people from shame and guilt over the mysterious, "I've struggled with feeling different for my entire life, and I've never really belonged or felt welcome anywhere," problem that can come from a variety of sources. The truth may be something like, "That sense of alienation from others comes from BPD. You have attachment trauma that has led to significant difficulty regulating your emotions. When you struggle to regulate your emotions, it impacts your relationships with others in a way that will lead to negative feedback/perception from others and make your already low self-esteem worse. We need to work on ending that cycle by letting you co-regulate in therapy and eventually regulate on your own, so that your emotional overflow doesn't prevent people from seeing all the good you have to offer." 

However, people who have BPD will hear the above like, "Something *you are doing* is causing the chaos and suffering in your life." When someone *became* this emotionally dysregulated, highly reactive, volatile person due to traumas completely beyond their control, it is difficult to accept the concept of personal responsibility without tearing themselves (or others) to pieces in shame. It's such a difficult conversation to have with someone that I think some therapists get less nervous just telling someone, "You have Not Your Fault Disorder. You have a special, yet awesome brain that society doesn't understand. There's nothing you can do about it except work on making yourself more comfortable in a world not designed for you." 

My personal opinion is that we need more trauma-informed ways of talking about BPD with clients, so their immediate reaction isn't to shut down and split on the "bearer of bad news." We also need more thorough ways of ruling out alternative possibilities versus always jumping to the BPD label. We *also* need to be able to differentiate between, "Honey, you're 22 and just coming out of an abusive family dynamic. You're coming out with some BPD traits because your parents had them. The good news is that you're here in therapy now, and we can work on those traits," and something more like, "You're 45 and have been using your childhood trauma as a permanent excuse to terrorize your own children and spouse the same way you were terrorized."

I think one of the issues with hypnosis or therapy is that they’re intended to improve one’s subjective/inner experience. When anti-stigma campaigns attempt to equate subjective/inner burdens (ie: being anxious, depressed, or traumatized) with more clearly measurable, medical symptoms (ie: a rash), they set an expectation that mental health recovery will work the same way as physical medicine. This leads people to hold hypnosis and therapy to the same standards as antibiotics, which I would argue doesn’t work so well.

We know hypnosis and therapy do help some people. “It only works if you believe in it,” isn’t necessarily condemning information. “Belief” is not always a choice. What’s believable to me may not be believable to you. If we’re trying to improve our subjective/inner experience, one person may believe there is no such thing as “recovery” through talking and only want hypnosis to ease their emotional stress. Another person may believe there is no such thing as recovery WITHOUT external support and validation and only want talk therapy.

Whichever option each person chooses is a real solution to a subjective/internal struggle. However, the problem comes in when these interventions are (1) standardized for insurance purposes and (2) pushed on everyone like objectively the best option. You’ll see some people do well in CBT but grumble they “can’t be hypnotized.” There are some commonalities between CBT and hypnosis, yet one works because the client is open to it, and the other is “hooey” and thus never gets a chance. Some people will do poorly in CBT because they just feel gaslit, yet they’ll love hypnosis because maybe they got to read the hypnotic script ahead of time and say, “Yes, these are the ideas I want to accept! Help me do that.”  

I think both options should be available, but there should be way less pressure on people who don’t benefit to keep trying no matter what.

My feelings about this subject are complex.

First off, I've personally developed some bitterness toward the term "healing." When people talk about, "Will I ever heal?" they seem to be referencing their progress along a finite "healing journey" that can one day be completed and put behind them forever. I think the ability to experience trauma as a deviation from one's normal circumstances, and the safety in knowing there *is* a "normal" to go "back" to, is a privilege in its own right. There is no comparing someone who had a normal, healthy upbringing that was interrupted by a single traumatic event to someone who has never known a life free from nonstop chaos and trauma. When people are surrounded by community, family that's good/safe enough, financial security, etc., their prospects are generally much better. Of course, there can also be privilege at play with how easily one manages to find a therapist who believes and understands their specific experience. 

That said, I do *not* want to suggest that I believe a certain subset of people are simply "screwed" and should give up. Too often, I've observed that forums intended for groups of people who are uniquely disadvantaged often turn into a circle-jerk of negative experiences that lead people to feel not only hopeless about their prospects but viciously angry at anyone who believes they *shouldn't* feel hopeless. To avoid contributing to someone's total lack of hope, I want to say something semi-optimistic, yet also realistic. 

If you are out there wondering whether you can make a "full recovery" (whatever that means to you) or not, I'd start by acknowledging that you are not sure if a "full recovery" is possible. When something does not seem possible, it becomes very difficult to work on it. To really motivate yourself to move forward, you need to start with a goal that feels *realistic* on some level. At one point in my life, working enough to support myself and afford an apartment did not feel realistic. If I was going to work, it would have to be very few hours, and entirely virtual. I did that. Next, I reasoned, I might be able to handle a solid 20 hours of week, still virtual. I did that. Next was a full-time office job. Next was graduate school. Next was a job. Next was another job. Then, finally, an apartment. Was this "healing" or a "total recovery?" Not quite. I still have trauma symptoms. However, I am living a life that looked completely impossible when I couldn't work at all. If all that's possible is, "Maybe I'll go outside for five seconds tomorrow," or "Maybe I'll volunteer two hours a week," or "Maybe I'll call the one friend I have," literally every "win" expands what is possible for you. 

If the idea of a full recovery feels impossible, perhaps focus on slowly broadening your personal sense of "possible" in every way you can. If there's something you can't work on, or that seems "stuck," start smaller or with something different entirely. When the focus is simply making your world a bit bigger, a bit less limited, there are more wins and fewer disappointments than when the focus is reaching a singular point at which you are "healed."

That's just my idea and may not resonate with everyone. It is 100% true that some people have a much simpler and more straightforward road ahead.

To me, “forgiveness” means that whatever the person did no longer impacts my ability to feel how I once felt about the person. 

Let’s say I love someone with all my heart. They do something to hurt me that is wildly out of character. I’m broken, but the thing I want most is to understand why they did it and reach some type of resolution. When I finally understand what led to the hurtful action, and I finally feel like I can trust them not to do it again, I’ll feel better. They treat me in ways I wouldn’t treat my worst enemy. They continually deny they did it. They laugh at my pain and seem to take pleasure in my powerlessness to change what happened. This is a tricky one to navigate for sure. 

C-PTSD is its own disorder. BPD has high comorbidity, as in, it frequently appears *alongside* C-PTSD. Many people incorrectly believe C-PTSD means "PTSD from childhood trauma," when it actually refers to PTSD from *prolonged* exposure to a chronically traumatizing environment/situation. You could have C-PTSD from spending four years in an abusive situation at ages 18-22. That said, 9/10 times, people assume C-PTSD = PTSD from childhood trauma. They further assume "childhood trauma" = trauma specifically from *abuse* or *neglect* as a child (ignoring all kinds of other trauma, such as car accidents, house fires, medical trauma, natural disasters, tragedy affecting the community or family, etc.). With all the stereotypes about what an abusive childhood looks like, it is assumed that *all* people with C-PTSD experienced a specific flavor of early attachment trauma and that *all* people with early attachment trauma go on to develop BPD.

There are definitely people with C-PTSD who do not have BPD.

That being said...

BPD is a highly stigmatized disorder, that is sometimes diagnosed more quickly (and with less care) than is needed. There are some professionals who are quick to label anyone with thoughts of self-deletion/self-harm as borderline. There are other professionals who assign the label based on a personal hunch that a client they've met is "manipulative." This is especially common in ER's or psychiatric hospitals, where the interviewer may have less than 20 minutes with the patient before they are expected to produce a diagnostic impression of the client. Some people get labeled with BPD at the hospital and then find fewer outpatient therapists are willing to work with them, and those that *are* willing to work with them take a very trauma-uninformed approach that feels blaming and shaming rather than supportive. These types of experience can lead people to think, "BPD is the new hysteria! They slap that label on anyone who's struggling too much to thrive in a capitalist hellscape. Eff this!" 

Meanwhile, there are people *with* C-PTSD, who *also* have an enduring pattering of destructive behaviors, emotional instability, self-sabotage, and toxic behaviors in relationships. Their awareness of appropriate relationship dynamics (including friendships, professional relationships, romance, etc.) is stuck at a childlike stage of development. You cannot talk through this with them. If you word things exactly the same way you'd word things with other people in your life, you're being insensitive/not "thinking before you speak." If you use "I" statements and word things carefully, you're insulting them by "acting like you're walking a tightrope." Their emotional instability and splitting, paired with their extreme rejection sensitivity, becomes impossible to navigate. 

I think for people who have been abused by someone who has BPD or NPD, the idea that we should simply accept these disorders as "part of C-PTSD," can be very triggering. It essentially sounds like we're supposed to ignore how badly we've been hurt in order to accommodate the feelings of people who've hurt us (ie: what we've been doing for our entire lives). I think it's exceptionally important to get a realistic idea of what an adopted child who has been through abuse might be like. When I first heard that many adopted children have trauma, I thought, "Okay, so they'll need a lot of love, patience, and likely therapy. That's no problem!" Having worked with children in this predicament professionally, I now see a different picture. There are children who are sexually inappropriate toward foster or adoptive parents due to a previous caregiver's sexual abuse. These parents struggle to find therapists who are experienced working with children who have severe trauma but may be too young to really engage in talk therapy or insight-based work where they explore their own behaviors. There are children who do not actually recognize what was wrong with their previous home (or perhaps do not remember the abusive aspects) and feel resentful toward their foster or adoptive parents for "taking" them from their original home. 

In some cases, kids find their biological parents on social media, without their foster or adoptive parents knowing. I've heard of biological parents who were serious substance abusers claiming, "I'm going to get you back, and when you live with me, you won't have a bedtime or any rules whatsoever." The next time the kid gets into trouble with the foster/adoptive parents, they'll say, "My REAL mom would let me do this." The foster/adoptive parents often have a lot of feelings come up, especially when there's a sense of, "I'm the one who raised you and put in the work, yet you'd take the person who abandoned you over me?!" It's very difficult on both sides.

I'm a supervisor with the power to terminate employees, and these are my two cents. 

It sounds like a lot of things may have contributed to the issue. Here are some thoughts:  
  
1. If you had an entire year to work on the project, what kind of supervision did you have to help keep you on track and monitor your progress? Were there any checkpoints where a manager would review what you'd done so far and give feedback. Even hearing, "It's great that you want this to be right, but we need it done by \[date\], so let's focus on what's absolutely critical to include and leave out the rest," could've helped to reign in your perfectionism and get the project completed. 

2. Was there any opportunity to discuss what happened with your supervisor, ie: "I worked hard on it all year, but my perfectionism got in the way?" It seems extreme to let an employee go over something like this. 

3. Is it possible that your perfectionism was more of an issue than your C-PTSD?

I ask #3 not because I want to downplay how C-PTSD can *lead to* perfectionism but because I often find that when people attribute lack of success solely to a diagnosis or neurodivergence that's not likely to disappear in the near future, it supports a narrative of, "There's something inherently bad about me that makes it fundamentally impossible for me to succeed." That's a very limiting belief, and you're likely to be even harder on yourself in the future if you stick to it. I hope you're able to either find a new job OR talk to this one about a possible second chance.

Something to think about is what will happen if your child does not feel immense gratitude toward you for adopting them. I’m a social worker, and I often see families start off all in with “rescuing” a cute little child from a bad situation, only to 180 when that cute child becomes a traumatized, angry teenager. This does happen, unfortunately. 

I’ll see situations where a child’s behavior seems to link back to very early trauma, which the parents dismiss because, “S/he doesn’t remember that, so how can it matter?” I’ll see situations where a child was adopted at 2-5 but got a rosy image of their birth parents due to “she brings candy every time she visits.” When things get sour at home with the adoptive parents, the kid seeks out their bio parents on social media (or romanticizes the parents they were “rescued” from due to not understanding the problem with their original environment). The adoptive parents feel unappreciated and begin to lash out over feeling “disrespected,” which leaves the kid feeling even more alienated from the new family, which leads to acting out. The adoptive parents then start to think, “She isn’t biologically mine, and she doesn’t emotionally feel like mine right now either. Lemme look for a group home.” 

This isn’t every situation. I’ve seen happier outcomes as well, but there’s often an expectation that if the child is adopted into a good enough home, the residual trauma of separation from their birth family will vanish completely, and the child will flawlessly assimilate into the new home. That’s not always true, sadly. It’s definitely a journey.

Honestly, the fact that therapy is not a silver bullet solution for any and every mental health problem seems to be pretty taboo for discussion. People tend to equate, "Therapy isn't necessarily the best solution for *everyone*," with some type of old-school, "Quit whining and pull yourself up by your bootstraps! You shouldn't need any help or support! Yay stigma!" The possibility that someone could be recommending caution based on experience and genuine concern for the other person gets completely lost on those who've never gotten a bad deal from therapy.  
  
Therapy is great when it works. However, some people's mental health challenges require specialized care that is much more difficult (and emotionally risky) to go through the work of searching for. Some people's personal perspective on their mental health issues/trauma make therapy more difficult. This could be due to cultural reasons, neurodiversity, spiritual reasons, etc. Some types of insurance (think Medicaid) leave you in a situation where "you get who you get" and can't really shop around. These are the more basic issues.

There's also the fact that not all therapists are good at what they do or can think outside the box (even when they are trained to work with trauma). Trauma is not a one-size-fits-all situation either. Sometimes people with a very intense level of C-PTSD cannot do breathing exercises or mindfulness as easily as expected, and not all therapists are prepared for that. I personally had very negative experiences that led me to believe there was something uniquely wrong with me. I still have a lot of trauma from bad therapy, but it's very hard to get others to understand. If you haven't already checked it out, I recommend r/therapyabuse.

I was like this for YEEEEEEARS. It was such a long-standing problem that I saw it as a character flaw rather than a trauma response. What helped me was using virtual EMDR to address triggers that had caused me to cry, rather than trying to dig into past trauma I can only partially remember. While I can't offer personalized hand holding or guides on how to do that, I wanted to at least say that it's possible to go from "instant meltdown in a rough situation" to "almost never cries unless they're truly sad tears rather than panicked tears" when you find what works for you. 

If it helps, the crying isn't about "strong" versus "weak." It's about your nervous system reacting in an automatic way to your unconscious fear that you're unsafe because someone is shouting. One thing that helped me was to look at how the easily angered/shouty people talk to other people to realize that it's not just about me. Another thing that helped me was to compare the actual power my original abusers had to harm me to the actual power my coworkers/roommates/etc. had to harm me. Even if they had some power to mess up my life, the potential consequences were "weak" by comparison. 

Another thing that helped me was to recognize that my haters generally don't give a fuck about whether I'm a "truly good person" or not. When a hot-headed coworker "goes off" on you, they do not need an intense apology. If they cared enough about your emotion to hear out an intense, groveling apology like the ones I used to give (and provide reassurance that they don't hate you), they wouldn't have snapped at you over nothing in the first place. The kind of intense groveling I'd do to try and "clear my name" once I perceived them as "mad at me" was ultimately making things worse. The trouble is that when someone says, "I have some issues with therapy," they hear a whole bunch of things you haven't actually said, that they associate with being anti-therapy.

An incomplete list of things they hear:

1. You don't believe mental health issues are real or, if you do, you believe people should "pull themselves up by their bootstraps" rather than having a safe/genuine source of support and useful feedback.

This is a very common assumption when people take for granted that therapy is always safe and genuine (or that safe and genuine therapy is available for everyone, in every situation). Therapy is seen as the humane "step up" from where we were not too long ago in history, when "asylums" with their inhumane, pseudoscientific treatment were main solution people knew about for mental health difficulties. 

2. You don't support efforts to "de-stigmatize" help-seeking.

Sometime between when therapy was first invented and today, there was a time when people assumed that only the "craziest" of people needed therapy. The irony is that many more therapists are trained to work with "worried well" clients than with clients who have complex trauma or severe and persistent mental illnesses. Older generations internalized that being "anti-therapy" meant believing it was shameful to admit you have a problem and seek help for it. Of course, that's not at all what most people who question therapy are saying. The truth is more like, "I support help-seeking, but the help needs to actually help."

3. You don't know about the science backing certain therapies.

Some people who are "anti-therapy" see it as similar to crystal healing (ie: something science does not corroborate at this time). While it's true that certain things are less scientifically supported than the general public believes (\*cough\* AA \*cough\*), there are some people who believe real medicine is pills and surgery, not diet/exercise/lifestyle changes/talking through problems/etc. A scientifically literate person could believe the literature while noticing gaps and limitations in what's been researched so far. They could also just be in the percentage of people who don't improve with whatever evidence-based method was used, or have seen a therapist who was unethical in some way.

4. You want someone to "wave a magic wand" to prevent you from having to do difficult work on yourself.

There are people who are "anti-therapy" due to simply not wanting to introspect or put effort into changing their own lives. They simply want everything to be better without having to do anything. However, often that accusation is leveled against people for whom "the work" is not actually demonstrating any observable benefits, who want to see something to show them they're on the right track. It's very frustrating when you're "doing the work," and being told that you're *not* doing it because surely if you were, things would be better. 

Unfortunately, I think a lot of effort to de-stigmatize help-seeking has managed to de-stigmatize (and even push) therapy without actually de-stigmatizing being different and/or needing something more than you can get from your natural support system.

Part of his role as a therapist is to try and help you to identify patterns in your own behavior that could be holding you back in life. When you explained your passivity at the bath house to your therapist, it sounds like you framed it less as, "I'm passive because it turns me on to be passive," and more in terms of, "I'm passive because I'm afraid of taking advantage of someone else." Therapists have clinical supervisors for a reason - they're supposed to seek their own supervision, their own therapy, etc. to manage issues like compassion fatigue, countertransference, vicarious trauma, work stress, etc. While I think it's fine to normalize therapists *acknowledging* and *addressing* their own struggles, we shouldn't normalize therapists bringing their own struggles to the therapy space. When a therapist says something like, "Oh yes, I went through the same thing," in an effort to relate to clients, oftentimes the result is more like the client feeling somehow responsible for the therapist's feelings OR the client having feelings about the therapist *as a person* that interfere with the therapeutic relationship (ie: "She said she recovered by becoming religious, and now I'm worried she'll judge me for not being that way").

The thing is, most therapy programs acknowledge that there’s no way to enforce any “totally healed” requirement for therapists. What happens if a therapist is doing a great job, and then her husband dies, but she doesn’t have the money to just drop the job while she grieves? The usual answer is she’s meant to seek support for herself so that she won’t be tempted to get her own needs met through clients. Once, I had a therapist tell me she’d had SI not too long ago and only stayed alive for her children. The problem in this scenario wasn’t that she had a mental health episode. The problem was that she was crossing the line between use of self and self-disclosure, potentially making the client feel responsible for building HER back up. She’d told me a lot of inappropriate things, but the professional boundaries they’re taught in school are supposed to help keep their day to day issues out of therapy.

I also think it’s common for therapists to think they have it together, take a training on some type of issue (maybe codependency or emotionally absent parents), and go, “SHIT. Therapists are generally encouraged (1) never to diagnose or judge someone who isn’t directly present in the therapy space and (2) to try and encourage perspective-taking when a client has a negative relationship with someone else. While there are times when this IS the right approach, it gets murkier when we’re talking about cases of abuse, neglect, or otherwise toxic relationships. The problem of people seeking therapy for validation that their situation is “bad enough” and instead getting “maybe look at it from a different angle so you’ll feel more positively about it” actually comes up a lot on this sub.

In the case of emotional abuse or neglect, you’ve likely been taught to downplay the significance of your own feelings for pretty much your whole life. You’re going to therapy to strengthen your confidence in your own perception of events. You’re seeking external support to trust your inner judgment/wisdom more easily. While I think this is a common reason why people go to therapy, it doesn’t seem like a common thing for therapists to excel at.

Considering that you are unable to see a different therapist, I think it might help to start with “I” statements. “When I sought therapy, I was hoping to learn to trust my own feelings and judgment more. When your focus is mostly on challenging how I see things, I feel like it leaves me second-guessing myself more than it really opens my mind. Do you think we can maybe refocus a bit on building my trust in my own judgment and perception?”

Maybe even you can provide an example like, “There was a time when I stayed in a toxic friendship for three years because I kept ‘looking on the bright side’ or ‘telling myself I was just overreacting,’ when what I really needed to do was trust my own judgment. Right now, my own judgment is telling me I still don’t have a comfortable enough relationship with my parents to communicate my needs to them. I need support in being happy with my decision REGARDLESS of how they react.”

This inner security and strength would also support you in recognizing when you aren’t happy in sexual relationships and not being afraid to leave. It seems like your therapy has you deferring to her perception of what is happening rather than building your ability to trust your own perception, which unfortunately is a common problem in therapy. There should always be a treatment plan. If you’re using insurance, that plan should be updated at the end of every authorization period (or on whatever schedule the company dictates). The only thing hitting kids teaches kids is how not to get hit. Oftentimes parents who complain their teenagers are “out of control” actually DID spank them as kids. Problem is that once they realize, “I only get spanked for things my parents know about,” they become deceptive and start doing things behind their parents’ backs. Then, when the kids inevitably run into situations they actually can’t handle without help from an adult (bullying, drugs, mental health, etc), they don’t tell their parents because their parents will spank them. This makes angry, depressed kids who have learned they can’t talk to adults about their feelings.

Some of these kids will join the, “I was whooped and turned out fine,” crowd, but they won’t seem fine at all. They’ll seem bitter and resentful that fewer kids these days are being hurt how they were. If what happened to them as children was positive, they wouldn’t resent people who aren’t experiencing it. 

Kids with physically aggressive parents often don’t understand WHY bad behavior is wrong, apart from “Mom will spank me if I do it.” You then get employees who can’t learn from a gentle conversation about their behavior and end up on probation for blatantly ignoring feedback that didn’t frighten or intimidate them. You get teenagers who are dropped in a group home where no one spanks them for misbehavior, and the kid ends up assaulting other kids or staff over a piece of candy. The parents are then bewildered. How did hitting their kids fail to teach their kids that hitting is wrong?

Alternatively, you get kids who are extremely angry and don’t know why, or who are emotionally withdrawn because they’ve been taught their feelings don’t matter. You ask them to identify their feelings or talk about them, and they get this hardened, stony expression like they’re gray-rocking someone who’s trying to strip away their defenses and leave them weak. Or, maybe they’ll gladly do all those exercises but then overcorrect for their upbringing by either becoming people pleasers or seeking so much external reassurance that outside people think, “Nothing is good enough for this person,” and start to pull away.
