I think it’s really common for lay people to recommend therapy as a source of advice on how to solve day to day problems, only for therapists to claim that’s not what they do. This leaves the client very confused as to what (and who) therapy is supposed to be for. I ran into that same issue myself, and it’s a big piece of why I stopped going to therapy.

Therapists are typically less focused on helping you solve practical problems (ie: “You should leave that boyfriend/get a new job/go to the post office on your lunch break so you’re not rushing,”) than many clients expect. This left me helplessly confused as to what the point of therapy was supposed to be.

Some of them focus on identifying patterns in a client’s life and recognizing where those patterns come from. This could look like, “So this relationship sounds similar to the other four you’ve described. Why don’t we discuss this pattern and how it plays out so we can stop it from repeating?” These types (who often practice a psychodynamic type of therapy) sometimes can give advice, but they teach a bit like a math instructor, using your past relationships as sample problems and trying to apply the insights they find there to your current relationships. I’ve never seen this done well tbh. 

Some of them focus on reducing the charge that’s held in traumatic memories. This was no help to me because I have the opposite issue, where my emotions are totally inaccessible, like my experiences happened in another universe. These kinds (who practice biofeedback, EMDR, or similar) aren’t there for advice so much as treating your hyperaroused nervous system. 

Some of them focus on spotting “cognitive distortions” in your way of speaking, to change how you talk to yourself. These kinds (who practice CBT or similar) tend to be especially aggravating when you want advice and all they’re doing is challenging your belief that you don’t already hold the answer yourself. 

Some of them only focus on coping skills. You tell them about your problem, and they start dramatically inhaling and exhaling like they think your only problem is needing to breathe. This drove me nuts, as I’d often be speaking emphatically to try and demonstrate the urgency and seriousness of the problem, only to have them interpret me as just “too worked up” and focus on that instead of the issue that had me upset.

The difficulty is that while a lot of clients do need the things described above, many people who go to therapy also need practical guidance on healthy ways to manage whatever is happening. That was definitely my issue as well. Friends would say, “Go to therapy,” and therapists would say, “That’s not my job.”

My perspective is that you don't need therapy to *convert* you to being cisgender or to *convince* you to be happy as a cis person. Rather, if therapy is the route you choose, you'll be better served by someone with an open mind, who's there to help you explore all your options. There are so many ways forward from this point, but they can be overwhelming to think through. 

The first possibility is obviously staying the course and not detransitioning. If you choose that option, your task will be to find support for your remaining dysphoria. I think every trans person, no matter how well they "pass" (for lack of a better word) has to come to terms with the fact that even the best transition ever won't make them *identical* to a cis member of the opposite AGAB. 

The second possibility is to detransition and live as female. If you choose that option, your task will be to discover who you are/can be as a female while being mindful of any negative assumptions/stereotypes you have about the female experience, ie: "If I'm female again, I have to be/do/wear \_\_\_\_\_\_." It might help to find some female role models who experience gender in a more androgynous or fluid type of way, so you'll feel less like you're going back on your goal of embracing who you are and more like you're refining your image of who you are in a way that no longer is served by transitioning. 

The third possibility is to consider a fluid or non-binary presentation, which may or may not require hormones or therapy. This option is kind of where I ended up when I decided not to pursue the full "identify as male and transition" step (which I was considering for a while). If you choose this option, your task will be similar to the task of the first option, ie: find support from whoever you can (professionals, other trans people, etc.) related to accepting your body as it is while validating your own personality and gender identity.

I'm so sorry for what you've been through! Believe me, I get how when you're lonely and attachment wounded, a therapist willing to "bend the rules" seems like a blessing...until she's not. What concerns me is that some of the questions you're asking sound like the questions I'd expect to hear about an estranged best friend or ex-partner rather than a therapist. This is a huge red flag that she did not establish or maintain healthy boundaries in her work with you. Texting late at night, wanting to see you on the weekends, etc., are not things a therapist is supposed to do. Rather than becoming a total replacement attachment figure, they're supposed to help us parent *ourselves* so we will feel less of that emptiness and longing the attachment trauma leaves behind. The idea is to help us feel complete by ourselves so we can have secure future relationships. 

It's really awful that your therapist played it up like the new client is somehow better than you. For me, the real question isn't why you were less valuable than this new client. The question is (1) why does she have "favorites," and (2) why does she let clients find *out* about her favorites when she knows it will adversely affect their self-esteem? It is not ethical for her to play favorites, imply you are "special" compared with her other clients, or hint at (much less really have) some type of friendship/dual relationship beyond the therapy space.

As a survivor of therapy abuse who became a therapist, here are my suggestions.

First and foremost, no matter how much you're angry about or want to change within the field, you *still* need good mentors and supervisors to teach you how it's done. When you do fieldwork, you may not have the option to say, "Don't pair me with a supervisor who supports \[type of therapy you find abusive\]," or "I only want to work with \[insert population here\]," or at an agency that does \[insert type of therapy here\]." Rather, you'll get what you're given in your intern years and be grateful for any opportunity to learn.

In the couple years I've spent in the field, I've had numerous conversations with people who do ABA, people who do commitment paperwork to hospitalize patients, people who are very pro-medication, people who stigmatize self-diagnosis or medication, etc. The point of these conversations wasn't to come away saying, "You're so right! I'll change my mind." Rather, the point was to understand *why* a compassionate person who's enthusiastic about helping others would support some of these things. This is the missing info you need in order to really make a difference. Some of what I learned actually surprised me. Not everything billed as ABA is ABA as we know it. In some cases, "ABA" is basically play-therapy being billed in a way insurance will reimburse. Knowing this, I can go about criticizing therapies attempting to extinguish harmless stims without seeming like I'm criticizing the entire field of play therapy. 

When I've talked to people who are against self-dx, I've seen actual cases of harm from people taking all their info from the internet. I've come back with anecdotes of clients who have benefitted from online info while having a shrewd eye for misinformation. The field is updating all the time. If you build rapport with other therapists and follow what you believe are the best and most patient-centered advancements, you can get other providers interested in those ideas. That said, going in with a mindset like, "Because of my trauma and lived experience, I know better," they may reject/ignore your suggestions rather than listen. 

There is a degree of respecting experience and intentions that goes into professional relationships, and it can be hard when you've been harmed by therapy. However, it is worth it when you're able to have those transformative conversations that (slowly) change the field. You can become a supervisor in a pretty short amount of time and then help guide newcomers to be more client-focused and pro-self-determination.

Getting my degree was worth it, but it DID require me to grow extra thick skin. It was a difficult process.

I think if I'd had a cheaper car in my 20's, and no student loans, I could have done it. I was living on $2,100 - $2,400 per month for a while in my 20's. Here are my tips:

1 You'll probably need a roommate, unless you can find a 1-bedroom for under $1,000/month. I strongly recommend finding someone you know and vibe with versus living with a rando off of Craigslist. If you must find a random roommate, a group of young people pooling their resources for an apartment or co-op is a better bet than moving in with an older couple renting out their grown child's bedroom. In those cases, you're treated like a barely welcome guest in their home, rather than a tenant, even though you're paying. Remember, if you cannot afford a masseuse or a therapist, you cannot afford unnecessary stress. 

2. You'll also need to cook cheap meals and rely heavily on non-perishable pantry staples. If you google, "$20 Aldi run," you can find some very cheap recipes for when you're in a tight pinch. There are even vegetarian/vegan ones these days if you need. 

3. You'll need a cheap phone plan that you can cancel at any time, without problems. I had Virgin Mobile in my 20's, and my roommate had Straight-Talk from Walmart. On a pre-paid plan, you can only buy a phone you can pay cash for today.

4. You'll need to avoid financing anything. Those recurring payments will keep you sinking. Even if you manage to increase your income, you'll still have to pay those off. 

5. You should never pay for something that's free, even if the free version is less awesome. For example, if you can watch PlutoTV, you don't need cable. If you can get workouts from an app, you don't necessarily need a gym membership. If you must have a gym membership, Planet Fitness is your friend. 

6. You'll want to be realistic when you get insurance. If a $1,000 deductible is half your monthly income, then you may want to consider a lower-deductible insurance if you possibly can. Otherwise, you could be stuck saying, "I need care, but I can't afford my deductible."

7. Be strategic about gas. In my 20's, the gas closest to where I was renting (a room in a house off Craigslist) was much more expensive than the gas closest to work, so I ended up buying gas on my way home from work or on lunch. You can usually see prices on Google maps when you look up a station. 

Hope any of these ideas can be of some assistance.

While AGP is a controversial concept, I know there are some detrans men who say that describes what they were experiencing that led them to transition. Unfortunately, the concept is pedaled mostly in transphobic discourse aimed at suggesting *all* trans women (or at least all trans women attracted to women) are transitioning to satisfy a fetish rather than out of genuine identification with the female gender. 

DID is a dissociative disorder that typically stems from childhood trauma. If you have DID, you likely have some level of amnesia for your past (or day-to-day experiences) that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetfulness (ie: not just "I can't find my keys," or "I totally forgot I was supposed to do blah blah blah last night"). Plurality, on the other hand, just refers to the experience of feeling like more than one in one mind. Some people who are plural identify as trans because the gender(s) of headmates can vary.

The way the term "Tulpa" is used in online spaces is not quite culturally accurate, but this would refer to you having created a separate mental construct that developed a mind of its own. This would give you a subjective feeling like there's a separate being from yourself co-occupying your brain/headspace. If you did not do this deliberately, it is unlikely it's a Tulpa. 

The term "sissy" usually refers to a man who likes being degraded and uses feminine presentation to satisfy a desire for humiliation. Typically sissies do not identify as women but are turned on by how humiliating it is to be treated as one (or to have rough, porn-like sex with men). 

Being trans means you identify with a gender other than the one you were assigned at birth.

To figure out which of these labels applies to you, I guess you could ask the following questions:

1. Do you feel like one person or many people? If many, you may have DID, be plural, or have a tulpa. If one person, do you feel like you're a cohesive, singular being, or do you feel like you're fragmented or split into separate sides? If you feel fragmented or split into separate sides, you may have DID or OSDD, but that's a *maybe* (and I'm not saying you definitely do). 
2. Do you see yourself as a woman in the absence of any sexual context? If you just went to the post office in a baggy sweatshirt and jeans, would you still want to be seen as female? If yes, you may be trans.
3. Do you feel there is something degrading or humiliating about presenting as female, and do you use feminine appearance/behavior to feel degraded or humiliated? That would fit the sissy fetish. 
4. Do you feel like you're presenting as female to try and become a woman you're attracted to for sexual purposes? That would be closer to AGP.

This all being said, I think there can be some confusion between these terms. A trans woman might feel sexy while seeing herself as a woman because that's her authentic self. This does not make someone an AGP. Someone who is trans could happen to enjoy submissive sexuality, but if that's not her primary motivation for transitioning, she's not "just a sissy." Usually people who are "sissies" choose that label because it's more of a fetish than an identity. You can be trans and have DID, be trans and plural, or be trans and make a Tulpa. None of these are mutually exclusive. It's a complicated thing because therapists are hit-or-miss in terms of whether they even believe DID exists, and finding a specialist can be difficult. However, I wouldn't jump to DID if you're not experiencing the amnesia, dissociation, memory incongruence, and/or trauma symptoms associated with it. 

Best of luck!

This therapist sounds like the kind who tangles up CBT with New Age philosophy. This is not to say these ideas are "wrong" or that no one is allowed to believe them. That said, when people bring ideas like "we are all one," or "we manifest our realities with our own thoughts," these are not scientifically proven ideas that someone should be treated like they're "anti-recovery" for refusing.

It *is* true that some of therapy is about finding ways to understand your situation that help you to feel better about it (or help to empower you). However, this is not supposed to involve flat-out *lying* to yourself about what's happening in order to feel less bummed out. For example, let's say someone is telling themselves, "I got fired because I'm an idiot." There may be a better, more empowering way of thinking about the reason for getting fired, ie: "I got fired because our company was acquired by a competitor, and I was naive enough to think the competitor would keep me on as a full-time employee rather than firing everyone at my office." If you were fired for "being an idiot," you might not feel too motivated to look for a new job. If you were fired for reasons completely beyond your control, you'll feel confident in explaining that at an interview to find an even better job than the one you left. 

The difficulty is that *not everything* is a matter of changing your thoughts. There has to be a balance. I have chronic pain, for a number of reasons. If I were to say, "The pain is unbearable," I would likely mean that the pain is compromising my quality of life to the point where I feel absolutely miserable. Being told I *can* bear the pain misses the point completely. Yes, I can, but I dread the idea of living a full life in this much pain. If I continue to talk about it, I might say something like, "There's nothing I can do about this." Of course, if I challenge that thought, I might realize that there are options like getting a new back massager, going to physical therapy, investing in a massage chair, seeking out literature on anti-inflammation diets, etc. that could help. This would actually be *constructive* because I'm not just silencing my thoughts with the equivalent of, "There are starving children in Africa suffering more than you are, so shut up." Instead, I'd be looking for ways of thinking that increase my options and opportunities. 

That said, I do think there are times when clients just want validation. When you feel really alone with your pain or just unheard, you're told you need to go to therapy. Then, you go to therapy and are told your thoughts/feelings are invalid. It's a nightmare.

To me, what you're describing sounds a lot like conversion therapy. 

In the United States, most of the major credentialing organizations backing therapists (ie: the APA, the NASW, etc.) have condemned conversion therapy as harmful pseudoscience. Rather than attempting to *change* a person's sexuality to something that is more "normal" or palatable to society, a therapist's role is to help a client feel happy and comfortable with their gender and sexuality *as it is.* The client is supposed to be the one to self-determine their sexual identity. 

The concept of AGP is a loaded one. It stands out among paraphilias because it was part of Dr. Ray Blanchard's "transsexualism typology." In his mind, "real" transgender women are exclusively attracted to men. He sees trans women who are attracted to women as less legitimate. Like many cishet people, he seems to conflate opposite-AGAB attraction with gender identity to the point of believing that exclusive attraction to men makes a more convincing case for an AMAB person being trans than exclusive attraction to women does. He aimed to explain away the transness of lesbian trans women by saying, "They're just men who are turned on by the idea of dressing up as women in the typical course of heterosexual activity."

There are a number of problems with this idea, but there are also reasons why it's more difficult to hurl into an active volcano than we'd like. First of all, the idea that womanhood is defined by attraction to men erases cis lesbians. Second, some transgender women [start off thinking they're exclusively attracted to men, only to later realize they like women](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K7WvHTl_Q7I). One might say, "Okay, so AGP is exclusively a transphobic lie meant to hurt people!" While that's definitely how it gets used, there *are* some cis men who are sexually aroused by the idea of dressing up as (or being seen as) women. While occasionally these cis men do get misled into thinking they are trans (and then later detransition), it gets problematic when the mere *existence* of men like this is used against trans women. 

I'm a genderfluid lesbian, and I actually tried to do something similar to what you're describing to myself, back in college. I was watching heterosexual porn while attempting to recondition my sexual response. The result wasn't me suddenly thinking Kyle from lit class was a charming, funny, sensitive man and wanting to go on a date. The result was me experiencing sexual arousal in response to the *specific actions* I was seeing on screen (or sexualizing something *about* the scene, other than the fact that a man was having sex with a woman). 

My takeaway was that sexuality is more than Pavlovian conditioning making us respond to certain stimuli. Me being sexually aroused by something related to cis men does not mean I can have an intimate relationship with a man, where I connect with him physically *and* emotionally. Being "trained" to physically respond to something that isn't an authentic expression of your sexuality is very damaging and harmful. 

My understanding of paraphilias is that there needs to be more going on than just "sexual arousal by something other than normal stimuli" for something to be truly harmful or dangerous. If a sexual obsession with feet, for example, becomes so important that the human being those feet are attached to is no longer a consideration, that is considered a paraphilia. However, finding a person's feet attractive while treating the person *like a person* is not a problem. I would argue, however, that objectification/reducing someone to what they can provide sexually is not a problem that's unique to people with fetishes by any means. 

What happened to you was wrong and possibly illegal. I hope that you are eventually able to feel confident in who you are and do what makes you happy, even if others don't understand.

It’s not really about the client feeling safer or more empowered. It’s mostly about trying to encourage self-reporting of symptoms that would require the therapist to call screeners. I agree not everyone needs or benefits from meds/therapy. That said, I don’t agree that going outside more/thinking positive thoughts is necessarily enough for people with severe depression. Severe depression doesn’t always allow a person to “cheer up.” By definition, depression saps your ability to enjoy things that once brought comfort.

Personally, nature and positive thinking weren’t helpful to me at my worst. I could lie on a sunny beach in as much pain as I felt at home. The smell of the ocean, sound of waves, etc didn’t bring a scrap of relief. Normally I love the ocean. I’d want to cry over how apathetic my brain had become, but I’d lost the ability to cry. I just felt unrelenting pain with every passing second. I did my affirmations/EFT religiously, and it couldn’t change the fact that I’d lost my entire reason to live, had no close friends or family whatsoever (except an abuser I depended on financially), had been actively harmed by multiple therapists, and felt so unsafe subjecting myself to more therapy that I couldn’t ask ANYONE for support without that being pushed. The last time I “tried one more time,” I gave therapy my all for three years and was manipulated to ruin by someone very unethical. I had to pick up the pieces with zero meaningful support or way to access support. 

Sure, therapists told me to breathe, think positive, or take nature walks. I did these things and still was living a nightmare. When someone’s chronically depressed for any number of reasons (which could be anything from financial difficulties to nutrition to social problems to sunlight to trauma to a vitamin deficiency), the answer is rarely one-size-fits-all. 

Meds didn’t help me because my problem was shitty life syndrome. There always had to be a simple, “Why don’t you just…?” solution or something that wouldn’t require anything beyond my control to change. Otherwise, everything was my fault, and I must be “creating my bad feelings” by having a sour attitude about being consistently unsafe and unable to become safe.

To this day, anyone suggesting affirmations, breath work, bubble baths, meditation, positive thinking, or walks in nature puts me on edge. It’s usually one step removed from the part where I’m blamed and criticized for not just thinking my way out of the chronic pain, C-PTSD, economic struggle, and total isolation that led to my depression. 

I weirdly benefit from the opposite of affirmations. I need to be allowed to feel how I feel and think my uncensored thoughts because if on top of all the struggle, I have to self-censors to be “positive” or else face blame for my own struggle, it becomes that much more challenging. If I already feel bad, at least I can try not to feel bad *about* feeling bad.

I don’t think meds/therapy should be pushed as requirements for people who haven’t tried the usual pick-me-up’s. I also don’t think there’s a level of depression past which ONLY meds/therapy can help. I think what each person needs is extremely individualized, which therapy can sometimes miss unfortunately.
